The plaintiff sues the defendant for, among
other things, a declaration that the defendant has no claim for fees or
otherwise and no claim for a solicitor's lien in respect of any proceeds of
settlement of the plaintiff's personal injury claim in which the defendant
acted as his solicitor and counsel at trial.  The defendant counterclaims for a
declaration that he is entitled to fees and disbursements and a claim of
solicitor's lien in respect of the proceeds of the settlement of the action
initiated by him on behalf of the plaintiff and payment pursuant to the
retainer agreement and in the alternative, damages on a
quantum meruit

basis.

Basically the issues relate to Mr. Waldock's
conduct immediately preceding and during the trial, particularly with respect
to his insistence that a
guardian ad litem
be appointed for the
plaintiff, which eventually resulted in a mis-trial.

The plaintiff lives in the eastern United
States.  In 1982 while visiting in British Columbia, he was a passenger in a
car involved in a collision resulting in serious injuries to him including
facial fractures and leaving him suffering from chronic pain including a
difficulty in swallowing to this day.

The vehicle in which he had been riding had
been rented by him from a numbered company which apparently was franchised by
Hertz U-Drive.  The plaintiff sued the driver of the other vehicle and his
cousin, who was driving the vehicle in which he was a passenger.  There was no
issue on the question of liability as his cousin had run a red light or a stop
sign.  She did not appear at the trial as I believe she lived in the eastern
United States as well and I also believe that the action against the other
driver was discontinued.  The numbered company defended the action on the basis
that the plaintiff's cousin did not have its permission to drive the vehicle
and therefore it was not liable.

Approximately two years after the accident
the plaintiff commenced proceedings.  The Insurance Corporation of British
Columbia retained Mr. Boyd Ferris, now deceased, to represent the numbered
company.  The plaintiff retained Mr. Griffiths, a barrister and solicitor
practising in Vancouver, B.C.

Following the accident the plaintiff
travelled extensively in Europe and as a consequence he consulted with or
obtained treatment from over 200 doctors in an effort to ascertain the cause of
his chronic pain.  In addition to that, some 500 x-rays were taken.  In the course
of all this, the plaintiff incurred special damages amounting to something over
$120,000 over and above medical bills that were repaid by I.C.B.C. for a period
of time following the accident.

In 1988, following the discovery of the
plaintiff over a two or three-day period by Mr. Boyd Ferris, the plaintiff
discharged Mr. Griffiths because he objected to being briefed for the discovery
by a student and being represented at the discovery by a young lawyer of very
limited experience.

He retained Mr. Waldock, who continued to
act for him until midway through the trial in 1988.  In his counterclaim Mr.
Waldock claims for fees and disbursements in, "... the action initiated by
him on behalf of the plaintiff."  This is obviously incorrect, but it is
of no moment.

The retainer agreement is in writing.  It is
a one page printed document with certain items being filled in and provides:-

The client
retains Oliver Waldock as solicitors to recover money for personal injury,
property damage and financial loss.  The solicitors will obtain an offer which
the solicitors are prepared to recommend or, if necessary, proceed to a trial
against the guilty parties.

The solicitors
will be paid on the following basis (cross out the two which do not apply):

(thereafter sub-paragraphs
(a) and (b) are crossed out)

Sub-paragraph
(c) provides:-

(c)for the
amount of the taxable tariff costs and 25% percent of the settlement received
or damages and interest awarded, provided that the fee may be increased by
another fifteen (15%) if no judge is available to take the case when set for
trial, such fees to be taken from the sums recovered.  See Sections 90 - 99 of
the Barristers and Solicitors Act attached.

Expenses
:  Jury fees, expert witness fees and other
expenses may be requested from the client as the case proceeds, estimated at
$15,000 but these should be recovered from the opponent at the end of the case.

If no funds are
recovered there will be no fees but the client will pay the solicitors'
expenses.

The claim will
not be settled without consultation between the solicitor and client.  If the
solicitor advises acceptance of an offer and the client refuses the offer, then
the solicitors' fee shall be earned on the offer, and the solicitors shall not
be found to proceed further without a fresh agreement.

(d)Retrials,
Appeals and fresh proceedings after judgment shall be subject to a new
agreement.

The plaintiff instructed Mr. Waldock to
settle the action if at all possible without the necessity of a trial.

The trial was set for March of 1987.
However, it was postponed.  The plaintiff, who had been living in Europe,
returned to Europe at that time.  A new trial date in September of 1988 was
obtained.  In November of 1987 the plaintiff returned to the United States.  In
February of 1988 he came to Vancouver for two weeks, and during that time he
attended various medical/legal appointments for examinations at the request of
the defendant.

On March 2, 1988 Waldock wrote to the
plaintiff's father, as he had been informed by the plaintiff that his father
would be responsible for the disbursements which were estimated at $15,000 by
Waldock in the fall of 1986 at the time the plaintiff signed the retainer
agreement.  He explained in some detail the disbursements he expected would be
incurred in pursuing the claim.  These totalled $115,000.  He then stated:

The law here in
connection with expenses of the lawsuit is that all expenses of the lawsuit for
professional witnesses, travelling to obtain evidence out of the jurisdiction,
transcripts and all the expenses I have alluded to above are recoverable by the
successful party.  In this case we ought to succeed in recovering at least
$100,000 and therefore we ought to be able to collect all those monies, if
spent, at the end of the case in addition to whatever the jury awards.  A
wrinkle or complication occurs if ICBC makes a payment into Court which is a
standing offer to settle the case at some sum of money more than the amount
awarded by the jury.  If that happens, then the Plaintiff is not entitled to
collect those expenses after the date of the payment in.  You do not have to
worry about that just now because no payment-in has been made.  When a payment
in is made, you and I will have to look at the risk of loss and the opportunity
for profit and balance it against the money to be staked in the endeavour.

The plaintiff's father showed the letter to
the plaintiff as he was concerned with the estimated expenses of $115,000.
Either he or his son the plaintiff called Waldock about it but the evidence as
to what occurred is sketchy.

Nowhere in the letter is it mentioned that
nothing would be recovered if the defence of lack of consent to drive put
forward on behalf of the numbered company was successful.  There is no evidence
anywhere either in the previous proceedings or in these proceedings before me
that any judgment against his cousin would be fruitful, nor that Mr. Kent would
have pursued this avenue or did pursue it.  Indeed, default judgment could have
been taken then against Kent's cousin, as I mentioned previously no Appearance
had been entered on her behalf.  As a matter of fact, judgment was granted
against her during the personal injury trial by Mr. Justice Lander.  At this stage
also, Mr. Waldock was not aware of any policy of the insurance carried by the
numbered company.  He testified that he was quite sure that the company would
have an extended limits policy.  He also stated that all of the expenses
"... are recoverable by the successful party."  He acknowledged in
his testimony on a question from the Court that it was his experience that
one-sixth of all such expenses are usually taxed off.

Discoveries in addition to those conducted
when Mr. Griffiths acted for the plaintiff were set for April 25th through the
30th of 1988.  The first date was cancelled however as the plaintiff was
required to attend a medical/legal appointment.  The discoveries lasted three
or four days.  Thereafter Waldock sent interrogatories which he had received
from Ferris to Kent, together with innumerable authorizations for medical
reports and records, which Kent completed and returned to Waldock.  However,
one set of authorizations was not returned and according to Kent these were
lost in the mail, but on receipt of duplicates he returned these to Waldock.

One of some twelve pre-trial conferences in
this case was held on May 26, 1988.  A portion of the report reads:

Items 6 and 7
relate to the list of special damages and the list of drugs which plaintiff's
counsel is in the process of preparing.  As special damages claimed are in the
order of $200,000, it was agreed that the list would be completed and delivered
by the end of June.

This was based on information at that time given
to Mr. Waldock by Mr. Kent and his father that they would amount to something
around $100,000 but not more than $200,000.

Following the April discoveries Miss Engel,
an associate of Mr. Ferris, applied for and obtained an order that Mr. Kent
attend for further discoveries.  One of the reasons given in the application
for further discoveries was that the defence had not yet received a list of the
special damages.

The discoveries were set for the late July.
At that time, Mr. Waldock met Mr. Kent Sr. for the first time when he attended
with his son in Vancouver.  The discoveries were supposed to last for four
days, but Mr. Waldock planned on leaving on a trip on the fourth day and as he
expected that a motion would be made in his absence to continue the discoveries,
he left an eight-page memorandum for his associate who was assisting him at the
time.  He detailed at length what had happened during the discoveries and
berated both Mr. Ferris and Miss Engel, his associate.  He concluded with the
following:

What makes it
particularly tragic in this case is that we have an A grade student, a graduate
cum laude from the highest schools, who has a mind capable of being a lawyer.
He worked in a law office for a year.  It is tragic to see him fighting his
pain and persons abusing the English language and the fine tool of cross
examination is being used in a way calculated to torment rather than to inform.

My view is that
the conduct justifies solicitor and own client costs, possible punitive
damages, a citation to the Law Society, a complaint to ICBC, a complaint to the
Attorney General.

The court reporter herself declines
to testify saying that lawyers are always doing it.

It is clear from the last portion of the above
memorandum, together with other correspondence and the testimony of Mr. Waldock
that, from his point of view, there was no love lost between himself and Mr.
Ferris.  As well, he indicated as much to the plaintiff.

On August 2nd Mr. Waldock wrote to Mr. Kent
Sr. detailing, among other things, a host of problems he perceived relating to
the plaintiff.  He concluded:

Jeffrey has
caused the following problems recently:

a)   he has occupied the phone at great
length;

b)   he has loaded up his schedule so that
he has:

1)   no time to do anything for anyone
else;

2)   no time to rest;

3)no
way to alter his plans to adapt to the next crisis or problem;

4)   no time to do necessary chores;

5)   no time to think.

c)he has
driven himself hard so that everyone else is shamed into working frenetically
with him;

d)charmingly
and gracefully been inconsiderate of you, me, my staff and others;

e)postponed
important interviews in favour of lesser priorities;

f)avoided
unpleasant but necessary tasks;

g)caused
you to join him in anxious reproach and stress of me and others;

h)blamed
others for his own defaults;

i)vented
his anger caused by Ferris and Engel by stressing you and me;

j)become
emotionally involved with his enemies over petty squabbles.  If they act like
snakes he should regard with detachment as curious reptiles;

k)   lost his sense of proportion;

l)impaired
my judgment in the heat of the battle.

The plaintiff replied to Mr. Waldock's letter
of August 2nd, 1988 to his father, setting out in detail his participation in
the lawsuit.  He concluded:

In short I feel
I have cooperated fully and at every turn.  I have come to Vancouver at each
request; went to any appointments arranged for me; sent to your office all
documents requested and never do I feel or know any instance when I was
inconsiderate to anyone of your staff members.

I tried my best
to respond succinctly and properly.  If I responded emotionally at times to Mr.
Ferris and/or Miss Engel, I would have been happy to have heard from you how to
better my response either before or during the discovery.  I would even welcome
now any suggestions you have to enable me to better respond to questions at the
trial.

We had an
understanding at the start of this suit, that my medical will always have top
priority.  I recognize that it is a difficult case, and that there are medical
and financial limitations compounded by distance.  However, there is nothing
one can do about these factors.  We must work
together
within the bounds
of my medical and the finances available to my family.

Mr. Waldock replied by letter dated August 23rd,
1988.

Thank you for
your letter of August 8, 1988.  I agree with almost everything you say.  I
think you have done very well and you have been most helpful to me.  That does
not mean to say however that you are perfect and it does not mean to say that
you cannot do better.

Nobody is
perfect.  I am not and neither are you.  Mutual friendly correction is good and
should be received in the spirit it is given.

Here is a list
of don'ts:

1.don't
let your medical treatment interfere with your lawsuit for the next 6 weeks;

2.   don't overload yourself;

3.   don't overload me or my staff;

4.don't
get emotionally involved with the opposing lawyers;

5.   don't expect me to be perfect;

6.if I say
I need help from you, don't get out of it by pleading other engagements.

You are a great
client.  I enjoy working with you and look forward to this case.  We have a
good chance to get a considerable amount of money back into your father's hands
and some for you too.  You have a difficult and challenging case but very
worthwhile.

With respect to the special damages directed
to be delivered by the end of June at the pre-trial conference held on May 26,
1988, Mr. Waldock retained his son to computerize the list which came to
something in the neighbourhood of $500,000.00.  This list was sent to Mr.
Ferris on June 29, 1988.  It turns out that this list was entirely erroneous.
It resulted from a failure in part to convert foreign currency to Canadian
dollars.  For example, 6,300 in foreign currency was entered on the list as $6,300.00
Canadian currency, whereas in actual fact it would be something in the
neighbourhood of $60.00.  In addition to that, some items were listed two or
three times by including not only the bill, but the receipt and as well the
credit card used in payment.  Eventually at trial or sometime during the trial,
the list was reduced to $120,000.00 approximately following a review of the
computerized list by Mr. Kent who, it will be recalled, estimated special
damages would amount to something around $100,000.00 but not more than
$200,000.00.

The plaintiff attended in Seattle between
August 15th and 20th at a pain clinic.  His father was with him but on the 19th
he came up to Vancouver and left his son's x-rays with Mr. Waldock's office.
Around the 21st August, Kent came to Vancouver.  On August 22nd, ICBC paid into
Court $192,000.00 in full settlement of the claim.  On the 23rd, Mr. Waldock,
without instructions from his client, made a counter-offer of $2 million.  He
described this as a "limits" offer.  Although Mr. Waldock testified
that he had gone through Mr. Griffiths' file, he was unaware that Mr. Griffiths
had suggested to ICBC or its counsel at the time that he thought the claim was
worth $250,000.00 and that it might be worthwhile to discuss settlement.  Also
on the file was the numbered company's insurance policy indicating a limit of
$2 million.  Mr. Waldock did not become aware of this either until late in the
day as it were.

Mr. Kent's father came to Vancouver on
August 30th and 31st.  They met with Mr. Waldock at the latter's house at about
10:00 o'clock in the evening.  It was Mr. Waldock's testimony that a large part
of the time was taken up with a berating he received at the hands of his client
and Mr. Kent Sr. over the fact that the

x-rays had been removed from their files and
computerized under certain doctors' names with which they were not familiar.
In other words, Dr. X may have been the treating doctor, but if he was a member
of a group of physicians, the x-ray would be listed under Dr. Y for no apparent
reason.

Also discussed at the meeting was the
payment in and the counter-offer of $2 million.  The Kents, after much
discussion, indicated that they would like to receive $700,000.  Mr. Waldock
proposed that a counter-offer of $1.5 million be made, but agreed on
instructions from the Kents to offer $1.4 million with a view to negotiating
downwards.  This offer was made the following day.

At that meeting or at about that time Mr.
Waldock discussed the appointment of a
guardian ad litem
for the
plaintiff.  Both the plaintiff and his father were adamantly opposed.

The personal injury trial before a jury
commenced on Tuesday, September 6th. It was scheduled to last either three or
four weeks, but at the commencement of the trial counsel informed the presiding
Justice, Mr. Justice Lander, it would probably take thirty Court days, i.e. six
weeks.  Notwithstanding that there were some twelve pre-trial conferences, Mr.
Waldock had some eighteen preliminary matters to be dealt with before the trial
proper could commence.  These related to a number of things, but mainly the
admission of certain reports and records and special damages.  Included in the
preliminaries was the matter of the appointment of a
guardian ad litem
.
This exchange took place:-

MR. WALDOCK:

And then also I
will ask for my client's father to be appointed as a guardian for this case.

THE COURT:

Why is that
necessary?

MR. WALDOCK:

Because he is
under a disability as far as I am concerned.

THE COURT:

It seems to me
that should have occurred at the very outset of this case.

MR. WALDOCK:

Well, that may
be so.

THE COURT:

Has he been
under disability all this time?

MR. WALDOCK:

Better late
than never.

THE COURT:

You could be
right about that.  I will have to -- that's Mr. what is his name?

MR. WALDOCK:

Roman Kent.
R-o-m-a-n.

THE COURT:

Where does he
live?

MR. WALDOCK:

In New York.

THE COURT:

New York city.

MR. WALDOCK:

The family home
is in Connecticut and they have an apartment in New York and he does business
in New York so he spends part of his time in each place.

Later, the following exchange took place:-

MR. FERRIS:

My friend said
500 items.  I think I said there was 200 doctors plus.  We have got this
situation where specials have come down from several hundreds of thousands of
dollars.  I think there was six or seven hundred at one time.  It's now down,
if I read the last one I got a couple of days ago, I believe it's down to
$126,000, I will leave that, I think we come down to.  So a lot of duplication
and extra trips have been taken out and whatnot.  It may be the present list
can be handled before the present jury.  As far as disabilities thing is
concerned, the IME's are replete.  My friend's IME's are replete, statements of
this intelligent articulate fluent young man and many of the paragraphs start
off and here we are in the morning of trial after an accident that took place
six years ago and the action has been outstanding for at least four years, that
we come here and he asks apparently to have his father appointed guardian ad
idem or whatever the proper term for the purpose of this trial.  There is no
affidavit evidence.  We come here.  We are caught completely by surprise.  I
want to tell your lordship that this plaintiff has been examined for discovery
on three separate discoveries two or three days at a time.  I just can't -- I
find it -- I am shocked when he comes along and says he wants his father made
his guardian.

THE COURT:

I want to
stress there is no jury present.  You have examined him, Mr. Ferris?

MR. FERRIS:

Yes.

THE COURT:

What do you say
about his ability to comprehend questions?

MR. FERRIS:

Without trying
to be smart-alecky, he is a very smart, competent young man with better memory
than I have.

THE COURT:

Brain damage,
is that the allegation?

MR. FERRIS:

There has been
some minor deficit in his very very high intellect before the accident compared
to his high intellect now.

THE COURT:

Did you have
him examined by a psychologist?

MR. FERRIS:

Psychiatrist, yes.  We have had
psychologists, yes.

THE COURT:

Whom am I
thinking about, Dr. Posthuma?

MR. FERRIS:

Shalman, they
are all involved.

THE COURT:

Are they?

MR. FERRIS:

It comes what
we are getting down to is did he have an IQ before the accident that your
lordship and I would have loved to have, and if he did have that, his IQ now is
ranged from superior to high average or something.  This is what the issue is.
But I mean what else can I say except when one reads the transcript through you
will have to draw your own judgment.  I have no difficulty with him
understanding questions or hundreds of documents put to him and medical
examinations or whatnot.  If he suffered an intellectual deficit, it must have
been in a very high plane.

THE COURT:

Does he have memory of the accident itself?

MR. FERRIS:

Doesn't have
memory because he was unconscious.  He has memory of the hospital afterwards.
Just lastly, I will set down, my friend has given me the plaintiff's final list
of particulars of injury this morning.  I will agree with them they are all in
his original statement of claim plus a letter that he gave to us adding
injuries that he said he was going to amend which you will formally do before
your lordship, and he has added for the first time, very first time number 19
the last one, frontal lobe damage.

THE COURT:

My goodness, is
the first notice you have had of that?

MR. FERRIS:

Yes.  Now let me be fair.  Some of
the more recent IME's my friend is going to rely upon have referred to that.  I
want to be fair.  I am not suggesting it's completely by surprise.  I am saying
Mr. Justice Toy said all right, you can let your friends have your amended
injuries and we got it in a letter form.  We have gone through all of the
discoveries and the recent IME coming in there has been mention here of the new
theory of frontal lobe damage and are we to deal with that, my lord?  Yes, we
are.

In the main, the day was taken up with
arguments and submissions over the admissibility of photographs of the accident
when the only issue was the question of consent to drive; the admissibility of
a statement by the driver, the plaintiff's cousin who was not going to be
present at the trial; the admissibility of innumerable doctors' reports and
records including those of a Dr. Stammberger, whose report was in German and
which had been translated but there was a dispute over the translation; notice
to admit and the fact that a report of a Dr. Hendler in May of 1986 was not
included but referred to in a later report; whether reports were admissible
under Section 10 or Section 11 of the
Evidence Act
and the implications
flowing therefrom depending upon which section of the Act was relevant; the
admissibility of I.C.B.C. records, the matter at issue being whether they were
privileged or not; the matter of special damages previously referred to by Mr.
Ferris in a quotation from the proceedings; the admissibility of an economist's
report, Mr. Ferris resisting the admissibility on the basis of the
Sengbusch

decision of Chief Justice McEachern (
Sengbusch
v.
Priest and Priest
Management Ltd
.
(1987)
1987 CanLII 2796 (BC SC)
,
14 B.C.L.R. (2nd) 26
).

On September 7th, the second day of the
trial, there was more of the same.  Submissions over the admissibility of
reports and records were again dealt with in relation to Sections 10 and 11 of
the
Evidence Act
.

With respect to the matter of a
guardian
ad litem
, the following exchange occurred earlier in the day:-

MR. FERRIS:

Well, Ms. Engel
pointed out to me this morning and I just want to say this quickly, that friend
made the rather very surprising, to me, move to say that the Court, that he
wanted to have a -- make an application for committee, that's a very serious
application, My Lord.  I can only take it my friend is suggesting that it is, I
don't -- and his client is not able to manage his affairs in this court case
and instruct Mr. Waldock, that that's a matter -- we've received no medical
evidence or any application from the Mental Health Act or the Mental Patient
Act.

THE COURT:

He is asking for a guardian ad litem?

MR. FERRIS:

And if he's
serious about that, it seems to me that's a matter that should be dealt with
right now; otherwise if he's right, he's got no one instructing him.

THE COURT:

That is a good
idea, Mr. Ferris.  Are you still instructed?

MR. WALDOCK:

No, My Lord.
My instructions are to withdraw that application.

THE COURT:

I think that is a wise move.

The matter of the admissibility of the
reports of Drs. Stammberger and Slavicek was also argued.  Earlier a pre-trial
application had been made by Mr. Waldock to have their evidence taken by video
tape.  This application was dismissed by Madam Justice Proudfoot then of the
Supreme Court.  A lengthy argument ensued with Mr. Waldock taking the position
that the objection taken by the defence to a video deposition constituted a
waiver or an abandonment of the right to cross examine.  In response to a
question of the Court, Mr. Waldock indicated that he wanted the Court to allow
the reports to go in and to tell the jury that they should give them the weight
they are entitled to because there was no cross- examination.

Also on the second day an argument arose as
to the admissibility of evidence of a Dr. Holly Stevens.  In this respect, the
following exchange took place:-

MR. WALDOCK:

Okay now, My
Lord, the last matter that my friend dealt with yesterday was a Dr. Stevens,
and Dr. Stevens saw our client here in Vancouver for a brief period of time.
She has not examined him and she is going to say that she assumes that nothing
much could be found upon physical examination, and she relies upon the findings
of all the other doctors, including the defendants', of --

THE COURT:

So what value does that have?

MR. WALDOCK:

Well, because
it's a question of interpreting the records and forming an opinion accordingly.

THE COURT:

What is her expertise again?

MR. WALDOCK:

She's the same
as Dr. Stammberger, a facial surgeon, an ear, nose and throat surgeon.  She
does this kind of operation which, where you go into the skull just below the
nose, and so she knows all about these things, and facial fractures.  She deals
with them every day and she's at Shaughnessy, and so knowing that Dr.
Stammberger might not be here, we -- would not be here, we arranged for our
client to see her in case there would be something in connection with facial
maxillary surgery which might need to be explained by her from the records, and
so we have sent to our client, we have sent to my learned friend, her view,
which is that she agrees with the opinion of Dr. Stammberger and she can
explain the anatomy, which is very complicated, and the procedures, which are
very complicated.

THE COURT:

But she has never done a report?

MR. WALDOCK:

She's never done a report.

THE COURT:

Never examined the client?

MR. WALDOCK:

No.  The only thing that she had
read, all the materials, and she agrees with Dr. Stammberger in connection with
that, with that evidence, and that's it, and if my friend says that -- if he
says that Dr. Stammberger is not here and can't be cross-examined, he can
cross-examine her and offer her for cross-examination, because she has seen the
same records and she -- and she's able to do the best that we can to help my
friend and give any illumination that my friend needs on this subject from
her.  It may be a second-best solution, but it's the best that we can do in a
difficult situation, and I shall offer her accordingly, because it would be
nice to be -- nice to be perfect about the matter.  So as far as the comments
of my friend yesterday, that concludes on that.

The foregoing exchange is quoted because Dr.
Stevens had in fact examined the plaintiff.

A further lengthy discussion over the matter
of particulars ensued.  Miss Engel, junior counsel to Mr. Ferris, had received
a list of special damages in June and perhaps further lists.  In any event a
further list was served on her just on the eve of the trial.  During these
proceedings, she addressed the Court:

MS. ENGEL:

There's a number of them.  My
friend serves that on me on September 4th or September 1st, and he says
"Here's our amended special list as marked by the asterisks."  So I
wrote immediately back requesting particulars of what that -- what are the
amendments, how am I to know what an asterisk is.  I don't even know if he's

At the heart of the dispute between the
plaintiff and the defendant is the appointment of a
guardian ad litem
.
This is governed by Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules.  6 (2) provides:-

A person under legal disability
shall commence or defend a proceeding by his or her
guardian ad litem
.

"legal disability" is not defined, but
it obviously includes infants and persons of unsound mind.

Sub-rule (7) provides that:-

(7)Before the name of a person is
used in a proceeding as a
guardian ad litem
that person's consent,
signed by the person or his or her solicitor, shall be filed, unless the person
has been appointed by the court.

Sub-rules (9) and (10) are at the heart of
the matter:-

(9)Where a
party becomes a mentally incompetent person and a committee has not been
appointed for that party, the court shall appoint a
guardian ad litem

for him or her.

(10)If it is in the interest
of a party who is under disability, the court may remove, appoint or substitute
a
guardian ad litem
.

Sub-rule (9) was the only one referred to in
the proceedings and this was referred to by Mr. Ferris.  However, none of the
submissions to the court at the time were to the effect that Mr. Kent was
mentally incompetent.  At one point during the proceedings before Mr. Justice

.... I wonder if I could make the

In the trial before me Mr. Waldock testified

who had given evidence at the trial before Mr. Justice Lander as to brain

would have been appointed under Rule 6(10) on
grounds involving something less than mental incompetency.

Under Sub-rule (10) however if an
appointment is made it must be "... in the interests of a party...."

v.

for the disbursements that he did send contain no details.  Furthermore, had he
followed his client's instructions to attempt to settle the claim, many of the
disbursements may have been obviated.  Mr. Waldock testified that it was not
possible to settle the claim as the plaintiff's condition had not yet been
resolved, as none of the physicians who were treating him could determine what
was causing the chronic pain.  However, during the time that Mr. Waldock had
the file, the plaintiff's injuries had fairly well resolved themselves except
for the matter of continuing pain.  Even when he went to trial, the plaintiff
was still suffering pain.  I see no reason, therefore, why he could not have
made some attempt to place a value on the claim long before the matter came to
trial and to ask his client for instructions as to the amount he wished to put
forth as an offer.

At the present time there is approximately
$31,700 outstanding in disbursements which Mr. Waldock claims.  Under the
circumstances, I would not be inclined to award any disbursements to Mr.
Waldock.  However, Mr. Kent as mentioned previously, settled

his claim for costs and disbursements with
I.C.B.C. at a net amount of $95,000.00.  This of course included funds that he
and his father have expended themselves in the course of the action as well as
disbursements by Mr. Waldock.  Subject to taxation, I will allow recovery of
the disbursements.  However, because of the matters relating to Dr. Hendler and
Dr. Stevens and the mis-trial, I direct that no disbursements be allowed for
any witness fee incurred by Mr. Waldock and any fees for filing the notice
of trial and each day of trial nor any expenses incurred by him in respect to
the preparation of the x-rays or the special damages.  The remaining
disbursements are subject to taxation as mentioned.

By way of summary I find the following:-

1.Mr. Kent
retained Mr. Waldock pursuant to the retainer agreement I have referred to.

2.Although Mr.
Waldock did not meet Mr. Kent Sr. until late in July of 1988, it was tacitly
understood that Mr. Kent Sr. would pay the disbursements and in fact did pay
disbursements amounting to $32,261.10.

3.The
disbursements were originally estimated by Mr. Waldock to be $15,000.  In March
of 1988 he indicated that they might be as high as $115,000.  Some of the items
mentioned therein, however, did not arise.  This was the first indication of
the extent to which the disbursements might go.

4.Part of Mr.
Waldock's instructions were to settle the claim if at all possible, without the
necessity of going to trial.  Mr. Waldock made no effort to settle, nor even
explore the possibility of settlement with defence - all that he did was to
make a counter-offer of $2 million which he termed "a limits offer"
after the payment into Court of something under $200,000 by I.C.B.C., which Mr.
Waldock later followed up with an offer of $1.4 million.

5.Mr. Waldock
acknowledged that he had a quite strong animosity towards Mr. Ferris and this
affected his strategy with respect to the conduct of the case.

6.   The X-rays were mis-labeled.

7.The special
damages claimed when apparently computerized and delivered to defence on June
28, 1988 amounted to over $500,000.  In reality they amounted to only $120,000
approximately, and these were not given to defence counsel until the eve of the
trial and as a matter of fact, even then the list was made up with asterisks
indicating various changes, deletions, etc.

8.In attempting
to have Dr. Holly Stevens' evidence admitted, Mr. Waldock informed the Court
that she had not examined the plaintiff when in fact she had.

9.Mr. Waldock
acknowledged that he was in some way responsible for the misinformation given
to the Court by Dr. Hendler about his records, but throughout the entire day of
the doctor's testimony, he did nothing to correct that wrong impression.

10
.The trial
went "off the rails" not because of anything that Mr. Kent had done,
but because the trial Judge ruled inadmissible the reports of Dr. Standler and
Dr. Slavicek that Mr. Waldock wished to have admitted into evidence, as well as
the evidence of Dr. Holly Stevens which the trial Judge ruled inadmissible
basically because he was informed by Mr. Waldock that she had not examined Mr.
Kent.

11
.In the eyes
of Messrs. Waldock, Chaster and Holmes, and one or two members of the office
staff, Mr. Kent was an exceedingly difficult client to deal with.

12
.It was this
perceived difficulty that led Mr. Waldock to seek the appointment of a
guardian
ad litem
.  He informed the Court that it was because of these difficulties
that he could not obtain instructions from his client, but I conclude that the
only instruction he could not get was related to the appointment of a guardian.

13
.The proposed
appointment of a
guardian ad litem
was not in the interests of the
client nor was it intended for that purpose.

14
.Mr. Waldock,
while informing the Court that it appeared that counsel may only withdraw in a
civil case with leave of the Court, refused to proceed further without the
appointment of a guardian and thereby breached the retainer agreement or his
actions amounted to an anticipatory breach.

15
.Neither Mr.
Kent nor his father would agree to the appointment of a guardian, and
consequently Mr. Kent discharged Mr. Waldock which he had a right to do because
of Mr. Waldock's refusal to proceed.

16
.Mr.
Waldock's actions with respect to computerizing the disbursements, labelling
the X-rays, his submission that Dr. Stevens had never examined Mr. Kent,
and his failure to notify the Court in a timely fashion that Dr. Hendler's
responses as to his records were incorrect, if nothing else gave the plaintiff
cause for concern.

17
.Mr. Waldock
suggested to his client that he (Waldock) attempt to "orchestrate" a
mis-trial.  He in fact succeeded by refusing to proceed further unless a
guardian
ad litem
was appointed for his client.

subject to the previous caveat that no disbursements be allowed with respect to

As to the costs of this action, Mr. Kent
will be entitled after taxation to recover his costs on Scale 3 and

I do not have the order in front of me, but
I understand that an order was made whereby 25% of the recovery of $325,000 is

of this litigation.  I understand also that the defendant claims a lien on
these funds.  It is not referred to in the counter-claim.  However, that claim

If I am correct in my understanding that
costs are also in Court, I direct that this amount together with the accrued

to be held for the taxation of Mr. Waldock's costs in the personal injury
action.  However, as Mr. Kent is entitled to the costs of this action as set

will be entitled to the disbursements awarded by the Registrar at court order

There are many allegations in the Statement
of Claim against Mr. Waldock, some of which I have not dealt with and which are
not germane or related to the main question of whether Mr. Waldock is entitled
to his fee.  For example, the plaintiff alleges that he has suffered damages
and loss, particulars of which include:-

a)Costs
thrown away as a result of the aborted trial;

b)being
forced by the circumstances to settle the Claim for less than its potential
value;

c)damages
arising from being prevented from recovering taxable costs and disbursements;

d)legal
fees incurred after the Defendant repudiated the Retainer Agreement; and

e)unnecessary
costs incurred as a result of the Defendant's negligent conduct of the
Plaintiff's claim.

With respect to sub-paragraphs (a), (c) and (e),
Mr. Kent settled these costs with I.C.B.C. for a lump sum.  In other words, he
did receive some costs and there is no evidence before me as to whether they
took into account costs thrown away as a result of the trial, unnecessary costs
or any damages arising from being prevented from recovering taxable costs.
Sub-paragraph (b) of the Statement of Claim was deleted by an earlier order of
the Court.  As to (d) legal fees incurred after the defendant repudiated the
retainer agreement, the settlement of costs in the sum of $95,000 must have
included some portion available to the additional fees and disbursements
charged by Mr. Kent's new solicitor.  As mentioned previously, there is no
breakdown before me as to the makeup of this figure.

In the statement of claim the plaintiff claims:-

(a)Declaration
that the Defendant has no claim for fees or otherwise and no claim for a
solicitor's lien in respect of any of the proceeds of the settlement of the
Action.

I have made that declaration save and except the
disbursements.

(b)General
damages for breach of contract and negligence.

The claim was subsequently settled for
$325,000.00 plus costs and disbursements.  There is no evidence that the
plaintiff should have recovered more or that he was required to settle for less
than the claim was worth as a result of any action on the part of Mr. Waldock.

(c)  Special damages.

These are the out-of-pocket expenses incurred by
Mr. Kent for his expenses and that of his father in attending the personal
injury trial and later in settling his claim.  Here again however these would
fall within the realm of costs settled with I.C.B.C.

(d)Punitive
damages for his misconduct resulting in mis-trial.

The
Supreme Court of Canada and Vorvis
v.
Insurance
Corporation of British Columbia

1989 CanLII 93 (SCC)
,
[1989] 4 W.W.R. 218
stated
that:

Although
punitive damages may be awarded in cases of breach of contract, a contractual
breach which would make their award appropriate would be rare.  Punitive
damages are imposed to punish, and the only basis for their award is the
finding of an actionable wrong.  Unlike in tort, where the injured party is
entitled to be made whole, in contract, the link between the parties for the
purpose of defining their rights and obligations is the contract the parties
agreed to accept, and the remedies open to the plaintiff must arise from the contractual
relationship.

and:

Moreover,
punitive damages may only be awarded in respect of conduct which, because of
its harsh, vindictive, reprehensible and malicious nature, deserves punishment.

While I have concluded that Mr. Waldock should
have informed the Court in a timely fashion about Dr. Hendler's records; that
the proposed appointment of a
guardian ad litem
was not in the interest
of his client; and that he orchestrated a mis-trial I do not consider that
these actions fall within any of the categories set out above nor do they
constitute an actionable wrong in the circumstances with respect to Mr. Kent.
His remedy lies in the declaration that I have made i.e. that Mr. Waldock is
not entitled to any fees arising from the contractual relationship.

(e)an
order that the Defendant deliver all records to Plaintiff.

All records have been delivered to the plaintiff.

(f)interest
pursuant to the
Court Order Interest Act
, R.S.B.C. 1979, c75.

The balance of the settlement amount has been in
Court since shortly after the settlement was reached.  It has been earning
interest and consequently I make no order in this respect.

(g)costs
of this action on a solicitor and own client basis.

I did not award costs on a solicitor and own
client basis (special costs) as Mr. Kent has acted on his own behalf for the
better part of the time since the Writ was issued.  There is no reason to award
special costs up to the time the plaintiff discharged his solictor.
